items.title: 1 is the first digit of natural numbers 30% of the time
items.claim: Take any 'natural' set of numbers — house prices, river lengths, populations, physical constants. Look at the first digit. About 30% start with 1. Only 4.6% start with 9. The pattern is so reliable that auditors use it to detect fraud.

options.text: Benford's law: for scale-invariant distributions, the probability of first digit d is log10(1 + 1/d). The math reflects that doubling a number (or scaling by any factor) takes longer to pass through 1-2 than through 8-9 on a logarithmic axis

items.reveal:
Simon Newcomb (1881) noticed that the early pages of his logarithm tables (corresponding to leading digit 1) were more worn than the later pages. He inferred something about how often various leading digits appeared.

Frank Benford (1938, physicist) systematically tested the rule across many datasets (river lengths, populations, atomic weights, baseball stats, addresses). He found:
Digit 1: 30.1%
Digit 2: 17.6%
Digit 3: 12.5%
Digit 4: 9.7%
Digit 5: 7.9%
Digit 6: 6.7%
Digit 7: 5.8%
Digit 8: 5.1%
Digit 9: 4.6%
Formula: P(d) = log10(1 + 1/d).

Why: many natural quantities span multiple orders of magnitude. On a logarithmic scale, the spacing from 1 to 2 (log 2 ≈ 0.30) is much wider than from 9 to 10 (log 10/9 ≈ 0.046). If the distribution is roughly uniform in log space, leading digits follow Benford.

Applications:
- Forensic accounting: real financial data follow Benford; fabricated numbers usually don't. Auditors flag tax returns or financial statements that deviate.
- Election fraud detection: ballot counts in honest elections follow Benford; many disputed elections have shown deviations.
- Scientific fraud detection: many cases of data fabrication caught.
- Image authenticity: pixel JPEG coefficients follow Benford-like distributions; fakes often don't.

Limitations: Benford requires scale-invariant data spanning multiple orders of magnitude. Constrained data (height, ages) don't satisfy it. Carefully fabricated data designed to fool Benford also exist.

The mathematical generalisation: any distribution with logarithmic density invariant under scaling will produce Benford's law for leading digits.
items.why: Random-looking data often follow precise patterns. Benford's law is counterintuitive and has practical applications in fraud detection. It's also a window into how scale-invariance shapes the structure of numbers we encounter.

items.title: sin(1 degree) is irrational
items.claim: Sine of 30°, 45°, 60° are simple expressions like 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(3)/2. Sine of 1 degree, 7 degrees, or most other 'nice' integer degree values are irrational numbers with no closed elementary form.
items.prompt: Why are most integer-degree sine values irrational?

options.text: Niven's theorem (1956): the only rational values of sin(theta) for rational theta in degrees occur at multiples of 30 (giving sin = 0, plus/minus 1/2, plus/minus 1). Almost all other rational-degree sines are irrational

items.reveal_title: Niven's theorem and the gaps in trigonometric tables
items.reveal:
Ivan Niven (1956) proved: if both theta (in degrees) and sin(theta) are rational, then sin(theta) is 0, ±1/2, or ±1. By similar argument, cos(theta) rational with theta rational forces cos(theta) in {0, ±1/2, ±1, ±sqrt(2)/2... wait — Niven's actual statement covers SINES specifically}.

The consequence: sin(1°), sin(2°), sin(3°), ... are mostly irrational. Specifically, the standard table of integer-degree sines contains only a few rational values: sin(0°) = 0, sin(30°) = 1/2, sin(90°) = 1, and their reflections (150°, 210°, 270°, 330°). Every other entry in the table is irrational.

This is one reason the SPECIAL ANGLES (30°, 45°, 60°) feature so heavily in geometry: they have simple exact values. Most other angles need decimal approximations.

Closed-form expressions: many integer-degree sines do have closed forms in terms of nested radicals — they're algebraic numbers — but the expressions are ugly. For example, sin(15°) = (sqrt(6) - sqrt(2))/4. sin(18°) = (sqrt(5) - 1)/4 (related to the regular pentagon).

For sin(1°): expressible in radicals (it's algebraic, a root of an integer polynomial) but the expression has dozens of nested terms. Modern algebra has tools to compute it exactly; it's just not a useful form.

Why 30° and 45° are special: regular hexagons (60° angles) and squares (45°) tile the plane with simple geometric constructions; the corresponding sine/cosine values come out as simple radicals.

Gauss and constructibility: a regular n-gon is constructible with compass and straightedge if and only if n is a product of powers of 2 and distinct Fermat primes (3, 5, 17, 257, 65537). This is why the 17-gon is constructible (Gauss's first major result, age 19) but the 7-gon and 9-gon aren't.
items.why: Trigonometric tables look like they could be filled with simple values. Almost all entries are deeply irrational, expressible only in nested radicals or numerical approximations. The 'special angles' of school maths are a tiny privileged set.

items.title: A hotel with infinite rooms, all full, can always take more guests
items.claim: Hilbert's Hotel has rooms numbered 1, 2, 3, ... Every room is occupied. A new guest arrives and you can give them a room. An infinite bus arrives and you can house them all. Infinitely many infinite buses arrive and you can still house all of them.
items.prompt: How do you fit one more guest into a full infinite hotel?

options.text: Move every guest from room n to room n+1; this frees up room 1 for the new guest; the original guests still all have rooms
You need a special infinite room

items.reveal:
David Hilbert constructed the hotel to illustrate counter-intuitive properties of countable infinity. For a finite hotel, full means full. For a countably infinite hotel, 'full' is not the same as 'no spare capacity'.

One new guest: shift every guest from n to n+1. Room 1 frees up.
Infinite new guests (one bus): shift every existing guest from n to 2n. All odd rooms (1, 3, 5, ...) free up — infinitely many.
Countably many buses, each with countably many guests: use prime powers. Existing guest goes to 2 to the n. Guest k from bus m goes to (the m+2-th prime) to the k. All housed.

This tells you about cardinality of countable sets: adding any countable collection to a countable set produces a countable set, of the same cardinality.

What the hotel CAN'T do: house the uncountable infinity of reals. Cantor's diagonal argument shows you'd run out of rooms.
items.why: Infinity is treated as a single concept. Hilbert's hotel reveals that countable infinity has very different properties from finite quantity — and from uncountable infinity.
